title: Gardens in the Sky: The Rise of Green Roofs
titleCn: 空中花园：绿色屋顶的兴起

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Look down on almost any large city from a tall building and you will see a landscape of grey: flat roofs covered in tar, gravel and metal, baking in the summer sun. Yet a growing number of these surfaces are turning green. A green roof is a roof that is partly or completely covered with plants growing in a layer of soil or another growing medium. The idea is far from new. People in Scandinavia have covered their houses with turf for centuries, because a thick layer of grass and earth helped to keep homes warm through long, dark winters. What is new is the scale on which modern cities are adopting the idea, and the range of reasons they give for doing so.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Modern green roofs are usually divided into two main types. Extensive roofs have a thin growing layer, often less than fifteen centimetres deep, and are planted with tough, low-growing species such as sedums and mosses that need little water or care. Because they are light, they can often be added to existing buildings without major structural work. Intensive roofs, by contrast, have much deeper soil and can support lawns, shrubs and even small trees. They are, in effect, parks on top of buildings, but they are heavy and expensive, and they need the same regular attention as a garden at ground level. Between these two types sits a range of designs that mix features of both.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the main attractions of green roofs is their effect on temperature. A conventional dark roof absorbs heat during the day and releases it slowly at night, which helps to make city centres noticeably warmer than the surrounding countryside, a pattern known as the urban heat island effect. Plants cool their surroundings by releasing water through their leaves, and the soil beneath them acts as a layer of insulation. As a result, the surface of a planted roof on a hot afternoon may be many degrees cooler than that of a bare one. For the people inside, this can mean lower spending on air conditioning in summer, while in winter the same layer helps to reduce heat loss.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Green roofs also help cities to cope with heavy rain. When a storm hits a city, water runs quickly off roofs, roads and car parks into drains, which can become overloaded and cause flooding. A planted roof works rather like a sponge. The growing medium soaks up a large share of the rain that falls on it, and the plants use some of this water or return it to the air. The rest drains away gradually over several hours rather than all at once. Engineers point out that a single roof makes little difference, but when hundreds of buildings in the same area are planted, the pressure on the drainage system during a storm can fall considerably.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Wildlife is another beneficiary. Even a thin layer of plants can provide food and shelter for insects such as bees and butterflies, and these in turn attract birds. Some designers now deliberately create roofs that copy local habitats, using stones, dead wood and native wild flowers instead of a neat carpet of a single species. In a survey of roofs in one northern European city, researchers recorded dozens of different spider and beetle species, some of which were rare at ground level. However, ecologists warn that a roof cannot replace a real meadow or wood, because it is small, isolated and exposed to strong winds.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Despite these advantages, green roofs are not suitable for every building. The most obvious obstacle is weight: soil that is full of water is extremely heavy, and an older roof may need to be strengthened before any planting can begin. The initial cost is also higher than for a conventional roof, and owners must pay for occasional maintenance, such as removing weeds and checking that drains are clear. Supporters respond that a planted layer protects the waterproof membrane underneath from sunlight and frost, so that it may last twice as long as an exposed one. Over the life of a building, they argue, the savings can outweigh the extra expense.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Many city governments have decided that the public benefits justify some form of support. Some offer grants that cover part of the cost of installation, while others give owners permission to build slightly larger buildings if they include a planted roof. A few have gone further and made green roofs compulsory on certain types of new building. Whether such rules spread will depend partly on better data, since many claims about green roofs are still based on studies of a small number of buildings over short periods. What seems clear is that the flat grey rooftops of the twentieth century are no longer seen as wasted space.

title: The Long History of the Ordinary Pencil

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few objects are as ordinary as the pencil. It is cheap, it needs no electricity, and it works upside down and in freezing temperatures, conditions in which many pens fail. Yet the simple wooden pencil is the result of several centuries of discovery, accident and experiment. Its story involves a remarkable mineral found in the north of England, a war between two European powers, and a series of small improvements that most of its users never notice. Looking at how the pencil developed also tells us something about how everyday technology changes: rarely through a single great invention, and more often through many modest steps.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The story begins in the sixteenth century, when a large deposit of an unusual black substance was discovered in the hills of Cumberland, in north-west England. Local shepherds are said to have used it to mark their sheep. At first, people believed the material was a form of lead, and this mistake explains why we still talk about the 'lead' in a pencil, even though modern pencils contain no lead at all. The substance was in fact graphite, a soft form of carbon. It was so pure that it could be cut into thin sticks and used for writing without any further treatment.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The graphite quickly became valuable. It was used not only for writing and drawing but also to line the moulds in which cannonballs were made, which gave it military importance. The English authorities therefore controlled the mine closely. At certain periods it was opened for only a few weeks each year, and armed guards were employed to prevent theft. Because the sticks of pure graphite were brittle and made users' fingers dirty, people began to wrap them in string or sheepskin, and later to place them inside hollow pieces of wood. This was the beginning of the pencil as we know it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Outside England, pencil makers faced a problem: they had no access to pure graphite. In the 1790s, when France was at war with Britain and could no longer import English pencils, the French government asked an engineer named Nicolas-Jacques Conté to find an alternative. His solution was to grind lower-quality graphite into a powder, mix it with clay and water, and bake the mixture in a kiln. The method had an important advantage. By changing the proportion of clay, Conté could make pencils that were harder or softer, producing lighter or darker lines. Pencils are still manufactured in essentially the same way today.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The grading systems that indicate a pencil's hardness developed from this discovery. In many countries, a pencil marked H is hard and produces a pale, fine line, while one marked B is soft and black. The number in front of the letter shows the degree, so a 6B pencil is much softer than a 2B. The common HB pencil sits in the middle of the scale. In the United States, a numbering system is also used, in which a number 2 pencil is roughly equivalent to an HB. Artists tend to prefer the softer grades, whereas engineers and designers have traditionally chosen harder ones for precise technical drawings.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other features were added gradually. For a long time, people removed pencil marks with pieces of bread, until it was found that natural rubber did the job far better. In 1858, an American inventor was granted a patent for a pencil with an eraser attached to one end, an idea that was popular with customers but disliked by some teachers, who believed it would encourage carelessness. The shape of the pencil changed too. Many pencils are made with six sides rather than being round, partly because this saves wood in manufacturing and partly because a six-sided pencil is less likely to roll off a desk.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In an age of laptops and touch screens, it might seem that the pencil has had its day. However, manufacturers report that billions are still produced every year. Pencils remain the first writing tool for many young children, and they are widely used in examinations that are marked by machine, since graphite marks can be read easily by optical scanners. For artists, the pencil's ability to produce both delicate and bold lines is difficult to match. Its survival suggests that a well-designed tool does not necessarily disappear when newer technology arrives.
